Hecuba. The queen of Troy whose prophetic nightmares foretold doom, and whose suffering embodied the human cost of war.

Hecuba was the wife of Priam, king of Troy, and mother to Hector, Paris, Cassandra, and many others. She was plagued by nightmares that predicted her sons' destruction and the fall of Troy itself. In her terror, she attempted to prevent Paris' birth by ordering the infant killed due to her visions. But Paris survived, and her prophecies came to pass.

Hecuba witnessed unspeakable tragedy unfold exactly as she had foreseen. She watched Hector, her eldest and greatest son, die at Achilles' hands in brutal combat. Then she was forced to watch as the Greeks mutilated his corpse, dragging it around the city walls. As Troy burned in its final hours, she saw her surviving children enslaved by their enemies and her city consumed by fire. After the fall of Troy, she herself was enslaved to Odysseus or to other Greek masters, carrying her grief into captivity. Her tragedy symbolized the collateral human cost of the war, extending far beyond the valor of the heroes who fought it. She was bound to Priam through decades of marriage and shared suffering, mother to Hector whose death devastated her, and sister in prophetic curse to her daughter Cassandra, who would speak truths no one believed.
